summary: Describes how SNMP messages are processed and dispatched within the SNMP architecture. It covers sending messages of different versions to the right message processing model and PDUs to the right applications, and defines the SNMPv3 message processing model. It replaces an earlier specification.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3412 explains how an SNMP engine builds and receives management messages. It defines a Dispatcher that selects the right message rules, applies security through another subsystem, and passes each message to its intended application.

subtitle: How an SNMP engine prepares messages, chooses their processing model, and delivers each PDU to an application.

tldr.problem: An SNMP engine must process messages from different protocol versions, apply the requested security model, and deliver each protocol data unit to the right application.
tldr.mechanism: A single Dispatcher selects a version-specific Message Processing Model, coordinates with the Security Subsystem, and routes incoming PDUs using their context and type. RFC 3412 also specifies the SNMPv3 message format and processing model.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3412 is Internet Standard STD 62. It obsoletes RFC 2572 and has been updated by RFC 5590.

today: RFC 3412 is Internet Standard STD 62, published in December 2002. It obsoletes RFC 2572 and has been updated by RFC 5590.

sections.title: The Dispatcher and Message Processing Models
sections.content:
An SNMP engine contains a Dispatcher, a Message Processing Subsystem, a Security Subsystem, and an Access Control Subsystem. Applications use these subsystems to exchange management information. RFC 3412 describes the Dispatcher and Message Processing Subsystem, and their interactions with applications and security models.

The Dispatcher sends and receives SNMP messages and passes protocol data units (PDUs) to applications. It delegates version-specific message construction and parsing to a Message Processing Model, which coordinates with the Security Subsystem. The RFC describes these interactions as abstract information and service primitives, not as a required programming interface.
sections.plainLanguage: The Dispatcher handles messages for an SNMP engine and sends each PDU to an application. It asks a version-specific model to build or read the message and coordinate security.

sections.title: One Dispatcher, Several Models
sections.content:
An SNMP engine has one Dispatcher and may have one or more Message Processing Models. For an outgoing message, an application gives the Dispatcher a PDU and the model to use. The chosen model prepares the version-specific message, and the Dispatcher sends it.

For an incoming message, the Dispatcher identifies its SNMP version and asks the matching model to extract the message parts and coordinate security processing. The PDU Dispatcher then selects the application registered for the message's context and PDU type. The Dispatcher also records message statistics in managed objects.
sections.plainLanguage: One Dispatcher coordinates the whole engine, while separate models handle different message versions. The Dispatcher uses the context and PDU type to choose an application for an incoming message.

sections.title: Sending, Receiving, and Matching Messages
sections.content:
To send a request or notification, an application supplies transport details, message and security models, a security name and level, context information, a PDU version, and the PDU. The Dispatcher checks that the requested model is known, creates a local sendPduHandle, and asks that model to prepare the message. If preparation succeeds, the Dispatcher sends it and returns the handle to the application.

For an incoming message, the Dispatcher records receipt, identifies the version, and drops messages it cannot parse or does not support. After the message model extracts the PDU, the Dispatcher routes a request or notification by contextEngineID and PDU type. A response uses its sendPduHandle to find the application waiting for it; if no application matches, the message is discarded and the unknown-handler counter increases.
sections.plainLanguage: The Dispatcher gives each outgoing request a local handle and uses that handle to match a reply to the application that started it. For new incoming requests, it routes by context and PDU type.

sections.title: Application Registration
sections.content:
An application registers the combination of contextEngineID and PDU type that it will handle. The Dispatcher uses that registration to deliver matching incoming requests and notifications. Implementations may let an application register for several context identifiers or PDU types at once.

Each combination can be registered only once. If another application already registered it, registration fails with an alreadyRegistered indication. An application can unregister a combination later; an unregistration request for a combination that is not registered is ignored.
sections.plainLanguage: An application registers the context and PDU types it can handle. Only one application can own each combination, so the Dispatcher has a single destination for each matching message.

sections.title: The SNMPv3 Message Structure
sections.content:
An SNMPv3 message contains a version, global header data, security parameters, and message data. The version value is 3. The header contains a msgID, a maximum message size, one-octet flags, and a security-model identifier. The security model defines the contents of the security-parameters field.

The message data is either a plaintext ScopedPDU or an encrypted PDU carried as an octet string. A ScopedPDU contains contextEngineID, contextName, and the PDU. Together, the context fields identify the management information to which the PDU refers.

The msgID lets engines match requests and responses, even if they cannot decrypt the PDU. A response copies its request's msgID, and retransmitted requests SHOULD use a new value. The msgMaxSize field tells the receiver the largest message the sender can accept; its minimum is 484.
sections.plainLanguage: An SNMPv3 message has a header, security information, and a PDU that may be encrypted. The header identifies the message and tells the other engine the largest message it can accept.

sections.title: Message Flags and Security Levels
sections.content:
The one-octet msgFlags field includes authFlag, privFlag, and reportableFlag. The first two describe the security level used for the message, and the receiver MUST apply that level. The valid levels are noAuthNoPriv, authNoPriv, and authPriv.

Privacy requires authentication. If privFlag is set while authFlag is clear, the receiver increments snmpInvalidMsgs and discards the message. The remaining flag bits MUST be zero when sent and SHOULD be ignored when received.

The reportableFlag helps decide whether to send a Report PDU when the message's PDU cannot be decoded. It MUST be zero for unconfirmed-class PDUs and one for confirmed-class PDUs; the receiver treats an incorrect value as if it were correct for the PDU class.
sections.plainLanguage: The flags say whether a message is authenticated, encrypted, and eligible for a Report PDU if it cannot be read. A message cannot request encryption without authentication.

sections.title: Processing Reports and Protecting Messages
sections.content:
The SNMPv3 Message Processing Model asks the selected security model to authenticate or protect message data. When processing a reply, it checks the msgID and compares security and context values with those cached for the request. A Report PDU can communicate an error counter and value, but the model MUST NOT generate one unless the request is confirmed-class or the reportableFlag is set when the class cannot be determined.

The actual security depends mainly on the security model and applications in use. The RFC requires msgID values not to repeat while outstanding, to help avoid replay attacks. Messages at noAuthNoPriv can be spoofed or replayed on an insecure network. The RFC also defines read-only counters for unknown security models, invalid messages, and unknown PDU handlers.
sections.plainLanguage: The message model checks replies against the request and can send a Report PDU when the rules allow it. The security model provides the actual protection, and message identifiers must not repeat while requests remain outstanding.
